cells.literature: [L] Supervised performance exposed large gaps behind high take-home marks: viva and live-demo averages of about 35% and 44% against 83.8% on take-home work in a 60-student module [R81], no invigilated-exam advantage for AI-reliant students despite higher assignment marks [R96], and, in a non-computing business course, failures rose from 2.1-5.7% to 18.4% after a move from a take-home to a supervised closed-book exam, although the change also removed all resources and added time pressure [S119]. Live checkoffs with verbal explanation let TAs confirm individual baseline proficiency [R95], and in-person hurdles were the only elements GPT-4 could not pass in a whole physics degree [S097]. In a test of eight engineering students, proctored scores were far below AI-permitted scores (26.25% vs 78.75%) [S101], invigilated tasks correcting LLM code exposed debugging gaps [R33], and random post-exam vivas were used to check exam reasoning [S009].
cells.dataset: [D] In one computing course, students averaged 94.8% on AI-permitted assignments but 86.3% on proctored exams, and 90.6% scored higher on assignments [D24]; exam marks spread more and agreed only moderately with assignment marks (rho = 0.53) [D25].
cells.interpretation: [I] Supervision gives the most direct evidence of what an individual can do unaided, although a timed exam shows they can produce answers rather than explain or extend their own work unless questioning or live demonstration is added.
cells.conflicts: In early 2024, grades on secure and unsecure psychology assessments were positively correlated, so the gap was not universal [S124]. Auto-graded timed tasks mis-scored some correct but unorthodox solutions [R89].

cells.literature: [L] Under in-person invigilation GenAI is kept out of the task: GPT-4 would have passed a whole physics degree except for its in-person laboratory and viva hurdles [S097], and face-to-face exams, laboratory work and in-person closed-book unseen exams are reported as not yet threatened [R03], [R54]. The items themselves are highly AI-solvable: LLMs averaged 83% against a student average of 54% on six years of ML exams [S009], ChatGPT-4 Vision placed in the top 10 percentile of a national CS exam [S008], and ChatGPT passed 8 of 15 computer engineering exams [S030]. Weaker variants are exceptions: lockdown browsers can be bypassed [R25], in-class interface restrictions were circumvented, including by transcribing AI code [R77], and unsupervised online interviews may be vulnerable to real-time AI help [S001].
cells.dataset: [D] With best-of-8 prompting, GPT-4 fully answered 85.6% of EPFL CS questions [D03], and AI resistance did not reside in question format [J3].
cells.interpretation: [I] Rated under its defining condition of in-person invigilation, the type blocks GenAI use, but the protection comes from the conditions rather than the questions, so online proctoring and lockdown-browser formats are much weaker exceptions.
cells.conflicts: No study directly tested covert AI use under in-person invigilation, so the Strong rating rests on whole-programme benchmarking and reviews [S097], [R03], [R54]. Because the items are AI-solvable [S009], [S008], [D03], any breach of supervision is high-impact. Lockdown, interface-restricted and remote formats were bypassed or judged vulnerable [R25], [R77], [S001].

cells.literature: [L] Face-to-face exams, laboratory work and in-person orals are reported as the formats least threatened by GenAI [R03], [S001], and in-person closed-book unseen exams were judged not yet threatened while non-invigilated essays were [R54]. Fully supervised tests are described as effective for authorship [R84], and expert guidance recommends securing key programme-level assessments through supervision [R68], [R04]. In remote or computer-based settings, assurance depends on extra controls such as lockdown and per-student questions [R89] or keystroke-log monitoring, which detected most instructed plagiarism with 87.13% accuracy [R77].
cells.interpretation: [I] In-person invigilation gives staff high confidence about who produced the work and that AI was not used, but the confidence weakens in online or lockdown-browser settings.
cells.conflicts: Lockdown browsers can be bypassed [R25] and in-class interface restrictions were circumvented [R77]. Online vivas are described as vulnerable to AI assistance and avatars [S104].

cells.literature: [L] Frameworks place supervised, AI-free assessment against foundational or certification-required skills [R04], [R19], [R10], with recall assessed in class and higher-order work set as take-home tasks [S127]. Supervised formats can target reasoning when designed for it, for example tasks correcting LLM-generated code [R33] and live checkoffs scoped to listed tool skills [R95], but item types vary widely in what they measure and in how vulnerable they are [S030]. Critics warn that a return to invigilated pen-and-paper exams risks narrowing what is assessed [R88].
cells.interpretation: [I] Alignment is good for foundational computing knowledge and skills but depends on design for process and reasoning outcomes, which timed product-only exams capture poorly.
cells.conflicts: Authors note that LLM-debugging and construction tasks measure different cognitive demands, which limits comparability within one exam [R33].

cells.literature: [L] Supervised, time-constrained assessment is criticised as distant from real-world tasks [R01], and authors warn that a retreat to invigilated tasks may reduce authenticity [R57] and narrow what is assessed [R88]. Practitioners rejected pen-and-paper exams as inauthentic [R24], and a natural experiment in a business course notes a tension between certification credibility and authenticity [S119], [S097]. Live checkoffs in real tool environments resembling technical interviews are an exception [R95].
cells.interpretation: [I] AI-free, timed conditions are unlike professional computing practice, where AI tools are available, unless the supervised task is a hands-on demonstration in real tools.
cells.conflicts: Live checkoffs in real developer tools were argued to be more authentic than written exams [R95]. This rating rests mainly on non-computing or partly computing evidence and on perceptions.

cells.literature: [L] Supervised assessment is usually the No-AI or Against level of AI-use frameworks [R10], [R19], and it appears as an AI-free lab exam alongside AI-permitted tasks [R93] or as the No-AI foundation in a staged model [R96]. Institutions pair secure high-stakes exams with AI-enabled coursework [S115], so responsible AI use is developed elsewhere. Supervised tasks can still assess critical evaluation of AI output, as with invigilated tasks correcting LLM-generated code [R33].
cells.interpretation: [I] By design the type mostly excludes AI, so it cannot develop responsible GenAI use on its own and should be paired with AI-permitted tasks.
cells.conflicts: Supervised AI-critique tasks can assess judgement about AI output [R33], although students scored lower on them without prior training.

cells.literature: [L] Technology-supported supervised tests can capture process: keystroke logs and code replay reconstructed how solutions were developed in an in-class test [R77], and a timed coding platform tracked submission history and audit logs [R89]. Live checkoffs make working and explanation visible to a TA [R95]. Conventional exams grade products, and authors recommend process-oriented assessment alongside them [S092], [R96].
cells.interpretation: [I] A standard invigilated exam shows only the product, so process visibility depends on adding logging, live demonstration or questioning.
cells.conflicts: Process-logging evidence comes from custom platforms and one in-class deployment with instructed plagiarism [R77], [R89].

cells.literature: [L] Supervised tests are described as effective but resource-intensive and hard to scale to large cohorts [R84], and security is described as too resource-intensive to apply to every task [R68]. Large deployments exist: automated multiple-choice grading was used in a statistics lecture of 120-150 students, mostly in online semesters [R25], live checkoffs ran with 237 students but with long queues [R95], and a log-monitoring platform sustained 200 concurrent users in a load test [R77]. A lockdown coding platform worked best up to 80 concurrent users and broke at 300 [R89].
cells.dataset: [D] Proctored exams ran alongside AI-permitted assignments in a single computing course [D24].
cells.interpretation: [I] Supervised assessment scales when it is auto-graded or uses existing exam infrastructure, but individual live formats and custom platforms strain at large cohorts.
cells.conflicts: Some authors call their formats scalable but report queues, overruns or tested limits [R95], [R89].
cells.cohort_note: Small (<50): controlled-environment testing is described as a quick solution, especially for smaller schools using paper exams [R82], and lockdown-browser exams were used in a course of about 25-35 students [R72]. Medium (50-200): automated multiple-choice grading was used with 120-150 students [R25], and a lockdown platform performed best up to 80 concurrent users [R89]. Large (>200): live checkoffs for 237 students caused queues and took about 80% of TA office-hour time [R95], one platform broke at 300 users [R89], and programmes are advised to secure only key assessment points [R68], [R04].

cells.literature: [L] Supervised tests need invigilation, facilities and timetabling [R84], and live checkoffs ran longer than planned and took about 80% of TA office-hour time [R95]. Integrity measures for exams need substantial extra question-writing, traded against saved grading time from automated marking [R25]. Growing supervised tasks may require recalibrating assessment volume [R04], and a lockdown platform reported reduced administrative time, though with little supporting data [R89].
cells.interpretation: [I] Marking burden can be low with auto-grading, but invigilation, fresh item writing and live supervision add substantial staff time.
cells.conflicts: A lockdown platform claimed a 68% reduction in faculty administrative time, but the results section gives only a qualitative quote [R89].

cells.literature: [L] Paper or existing invigilated exams need little change: controlling the environment is described as a quick, satisfactory solution, especially for smaller schools [R82], and strategic in-person assessment at year end is proposed rather than everywhere [S097]. Implementation cost falls mainly on staff time and infrastructure: supervised tests need invigilation, facilities and timetabling, and interviews are costed at about 1,000 minutes of staff time for 100 students [R84]; live checkoffs took about 80% of TA office-hour time and needed Docker environments [R95]; and secure exams need extra question-writing and instructor availability when lockdown browsers fail [R25]. Computer-based variants need custom platforms such as a monitored web editor [R77] or a lockdown system [R89], one programme freed resources for secured code reviews by removing a first-year exam [R68], and staff resistance, resource limits and accreditation are named as barriers [R04], [R68].
cells.interpretation: [I] Paper or existing invigilated exams need little change, but invigilation, venues and staff time are real costs, and secure computer-based testing and programme-level redesign need platform and policy work; no study reported venue or licence costs in money terms, so cost evidence is limited to staff time and infrastructure descriptions.
cells.conflicts: An open-book supervised exam needed Head of Department or Academic Council approval and extra preparation [S009].

cells.literature: [L] Supervision removes advantages from unequal AI access, a concern raised by instructors (32% worried about unfairness between AI users and non-users) [S342], by students [S101] and in benchmarking where paid tools beat free ones [S001], [R10]. Against this, guidelines caution that over-reliance on in-class or oral formats may disadvantage non-native speakers and students with disabilities [R51], high-stakes supervised testing can cause stress [R84], lockdown browsers malfunctioned for about 2-3% of students [R25], and monitoring falsely flagged honest students with atypical editing styles [R77]. Accommodations such as extra time and read-aloud questions can mitigate some of this [S009], [R95].
cells.interpretation: [I] Supervised assessment is fairer on AI access but can disadvantage anxious students, students with disabilities and those affected by technical failures unless accommodations are planned.
cells.conflicts: Evidence points in both directions: equity of AI access improves, but stress, accommodation and technical-failure risks rise [R51], [R84], [R25].

evaluation_finding: Supervised assessment gives the most credible evidence of individual unaided capability and authorship, and supervised results repeatedly revealed gaps that AI-permitted work concealed [R81], [R96], [D24], with confounded non-computing support [S119]. Under in-person invigilation it keeps GenAI out of the task, but this security comes from the conditions rather than the questions, which current models can largely answer [S097], [S009], [S008], [J3], and lockdown or online variants are much weaker [R25], [R77]. It scores poorly on authenticity and on developing responsible AI use [R01], [R10], carries real invigilation and staff-time costs [R84], [R95], and works best as a targeted gatekeeping component within a programme that also uses AI-permitted, process-focused tasks [R68], [R04], [S115].
strengths: Supervised vivas, demonstrations and exams exposed large gaps between take-home marks and individual capability [R81], [R96], [D24], and confounded grade data from a non-computing course point the same way [S119].

Under in-person invigilation GenAI is kept out of the task: in-person hurdles were the only elements that GPT-4 could not pass across a whole degree [S097], and face-to-face formats are reported as least threatened by GenAI [R03], [S001].
It removes unfairness from unequal access to paid or advanced AI tools [S342], [S001], [R10].
Live checkoffs in real developer tools combine supervision with demonstration and explanation and were valued by students [R95].
limitations: Exam items themselves are highly AI-solvable, so any breach of supervision is high-impact, and no study directly tested covert AI use under in-person invigilation [S009], [S008], [S030], [D03].
Lockdown browsers and interface restrictions can be bypassed or circumvented, so online and lockdown variants do not share the in-person rating [R25], [R77].
Timed, AI-free conditions are criticised as inauthentic and as narrowing what is assessed [R01], [R57], [R88], [R24].
The type mostly excludes AI, so it does not develop responsible GenAI use on its own [R10], [R19].

Invigilation, facilities, timetabling and live supervision carry substantial staff-time costs at scale [R84], [R95], and over-reliance on in-class formats may disadvantage non-native speakers, students with disabilities and anxious students [R51], [R84].
practical_considerations: Secure selected gatekeeping or stage-gate assessments rather than every task, because supervision is resource-intensive; one programme funded secured code reviews by removing a first-year exam [R68], [R04], [S097].
For large cohorts, prefer auto-graded or existing invigilated exams; live checkoffs at 237 students took about 80% of TA office-hour time [R95], [R25].
Budget for invigilation, venues and timetabling, and for custom platforms if testing is computer-based, since lockdown and monitoring tools need their own infrastructure [R84], [R77], [R89].
Write fresh or parameter-modified items and pre-test them against GenAI, accepting the extra preparation effort [R25], [S008], [R51].
Pair supervised components with AI-permitted coursework and short questioning, and plan accommodations, quieter spaces and fallbacks for technical failures [S115], [R93], [S009], [R95], [R25].
evidence_gaps: No study directly compared the learning effects of supervised versus AI-permitted assessment in computing with a controlled design.
No study directly tested how often students covertly use GenAI under in-person invigilation.
Evidence on remote or online proctoring security under current GenAI tools is thin and mostly anecdotal or from instructed-cheating evaluations.
Staff workload and monetary costs (venues, invigilators, licences) for invigilated computing exams at large cohorts (>200) were not measured.
The effect of supervised AI-critique tasks on students who received prior training was not tested.
Equity impacts on specific groups (students with disabilities, English as an additional language) were not measured for supervised computing assessments.
